chapter: Boots and His Buddies and Wild Cherry
title: Oberstein records the reworked tune and Harris becomes Joe Harris
summary: At the session the band plays the new version; Oberstein calls it an original, and Harris, asked for his name, takes the popular nickname Joe, so the record credits Joe Harris.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: He said, yeah man, but let him play what he's been playing today on this thing. We had no record on the music. We said, oh man, we've got some stocks here we've got to run over. Finally they got around to it. He said, let him play it man. Well they played it, the guy said, yeah man, that thing is crazy. Well they all fell in and got the harmony and everything. Well they went back and got this arrangement, oh wait a minute, listen to what this chord is here. Well we used some of the same chords in this thing, in this arrangement, but we played it maybe slower, instead of this thing was fast and screaming, one of those screaming was the right chords, you know. He used to write music to kill the brass, you know. Well I changed that all around, see. I changed the darn thing, I almost changed the melody, you know. So they liked it. When Oberstein heard it, he said, that's an original. So I said, well where did you get that song? I got my idea, Cherries. He said, well you can't call that Cherries too, they're not the same number. It's a different tempo, it's a different mood. When I went right away, when I was talking, I didn't know he was an experienced musician, he was talking about the moods and the movements, and it's all right. He did. He changed. Made the record of it, played it back. It sounded terrific man, it was good, it didn't sound like the same.
It can't be, play it again.

So I listened to it. That was it. Well when he got through he came to me, he says, or he went to Boots, he says, Boots, who's number is that? I was looking around. He says, L.D., he says, I did. I said, well I don't know. Somebody's got a claiming number. I said, I don't know. I just, well okay, it's my number. I said, what's your name? He says, these guy's writing. My name was Lawrence Douglas Harris. I said, well what if I said L.D.? My name was L.D., I said, I don't know what's your name. I said, well that's too long. I said, well that's too long. At that time, Joe was the popular name of the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. I asked him to go to the guy. At that time Joe was the popular name, all the musicians, they called him Joe. Somebody, Troy, no I wasn't Troy, Jimmy Lusford had made a number of, Joe plays and so and so in the band. The name Joe stuck to the musicians. Everybody wanted to be called Joe. I said Joe Harris. Okay, that's all right, Joe Harris was new. Well he wrote Joe Harris. And that's on the record right today. Pooch and his buddies, Joe Harris of course. I don't know how much I got out of it.
